q: Why is my MSME loan rate linked to the repo rate, and when should it fall after an RBI rate cut?
title: Repo-linked MSME loans after a rate cut
short: RBI requires banks to link new floating rate loans to micro and small enterprises to an external benchmark, most often the repo rate, so rate changes pass through. After a cut, your rate falls on your loan's next reset date, which must come at least once every three months.
audience: MSME borrowers on floating rate loans

p: RBI's circular of 4 September 2019 made banks link all new floating rate loans to micro and small enterprises, from 1 October 2019, to an external benchmark: the RBI repo rate, a government Treasury bill yield published by FBIL, or another FBIL benchmark. Floating rate loans to medium enterprises followed from 1 April 2020. Each bank picks the benchmark, but must use one benchmark within a loan category.

ul: Your rate = benchmark + spread. With a repo-linked loan, the benchmark moves only when RBI changes the repo rate.
Reset: the rate must be reset at least once every three months. Your sanction letter states the reset dates.
Credit risk premium: can change only if your credit assessment changes substantially, as agreed in the loan contract.
Other parts of the spread: can be raised only once in three years. Since 1 October 2025 a bank may cut them sooner in the borrower's favour, under its board-approved policy.

p: On the first reset date after the repo cut. If your loan resets quarterly and the cut came just after a reset, you may wait close to three months. The bank may keep your EMI and shorten the tenure, or cut the EMI; ask which, and ask for the revised repayment schedule in writing. Some banks also offer a switch to a fixed rate at reset, at their discretion.

sections.h: Loans that do not follow the repo rate
ul: Older loans on MCLR or base rate reset on their own schedule, often yearly, and pass on cuts more slowly. You can ask to switch to the external benchmark; the bank may charge a fee and the new spread is agreed between you.
Fixed rate loans do not change.
Loans from NBFCs: the external benchmark rule was issued to banks, so an NBFC loan moves as its agreement says. Read the reset clause before you sign.

example.title: Worked example: a 25 basis point cut (rates assumed)
lines: RBI cuts repo by 0.25%: new rate 5.25% + 3.50% = 8.75% from the next reset
Interest saved in a year on the same balance: 50,00,000 x 0.25% = ₹12,500
example.note: Repo and spread are illustrative, not the current rates. Your saving depends on the balance outstanding and the reset date.

senseible: Your loan rate is set by your bank under RBI rules. If the loan is a green loan with sustainability reporting, Senseible keeps the bill-backed emission records the lender may ask for after disbursement.
